title: Constant-time maximum with restoration
stem: A stack S supports PUSH, POP and TOP. Design FIND-MAX(S) to return the largest currently stored value efficiently. Which proposed approach is correct and efficient?
options: Maintain one MAX variable on PUSH. FIND-MAX is constant time, but rebuilding MAX after a POP needs linear time.
Each FIND-MAX pops all elements, computes the maximum, and restores the original order. Each query is linear.
On every PUSH, an auxiliary stack M stores the maximum of the prefix then present in S. A POP also removes M's top. FIND-MAX is constant time.
On every PUSH, recursively compute the maximum of the current stack and append it to S. FIND-MAX takes logarithmic time.
solution:
Option 3 stores one cached maximum per data-stack prefix. Induction proves each M entry is the maximum of the corresponding S prefix; synchronous POP exposes the prior valid prefix. PUSH, POP, TOP of M and FIND-MAX all use constant operations, and M uses O(n) space. Duplicates are retained because every push stores a prefix result. Option 1 explicitly needs a linear rebuild after removing the current maximum, so it does not give the same complete efficient interface. Option 2 preserves the answer and order only with restoration storage but scans on every query. Option 4 adds metadata as if it were data and gives no valid logarithmic recurrence. Empty-stack maximum must have a specified error/identity policy. This is an independently derived answer, not an official key.

**Amortization test.** Repeated FIND-MAX calls that pop and restore the same n records each cost linear time: restoration recreates the work rather than consuming it permanently. N such calls cost Theta(Nn). The prefix-max metadata construction instead gives constant worst-case calls; it does not rely on amortizing repeated full scans.

title: Sequential merge versus a heap-head frontier
stem: There are $k$ sorted lists, each containing $n/k$ elements. Merge lists 1 and 2, then merge the result with list 3, and continue in this way. What is the worst-case running-time bound of this algorithm?
solution:
1. At stage $j$, merge an accumulated list of $j n/k$ elements with the next list of $n/k$ elements. In the standard linear-time merge model, the worst-case work is proportional to $(j+1)n/k$.
2. Sum the stage costs for $j=1,\ldots,k-1$: $(n/k)(2+3+\cdots+k)=(n/k)(k(k+1)/2-1)$. For $2\le k\le n$, this is $\Theta(nk)$, so option 4 is the stated bound.
3. A balanced merge tree instead processes all $n$ elements at each of $\Theta(\log k)$ levels and takes $\Theta(n\log k)$. A heap can achieve the same asymptotic bound, but neither is the sequential algorithm in the question.
4. The worst case includes inputs whose keys remain interleaved at successive merges; one cannot price every stage at the size of the incoming list alone. If $k$ is fixed independently of $n$, the expression becomes linear in $n$, but the listed options treat both parameters as variable.

**Transfer rule.** Write the accumulated problem size at each iteration before summing costs. A correct bound for a different merge strategy is a distractor, not an answer.

**Amortization test.** Sequential accumulation revisits old elements in many later merges, creating an arithmetic sum. Binary-level rebuilding lets each record participate only once per level, creating logarithmic amortized insertion. The different total bounds follow from different lifetime participation counts, not the word merge alone.
pattern: growing work per iteration and two-parameter cost
